about: Reference recordings of wild turkey (Meleagris gallopavo). Licenses were checked on each recording's own page. trimStartSec/trimEndSec are seconds in the original file as downloaded. Each clip keeps at least 0.3 s before the call for the noise floor.

clips.author: Jonathon Jongsma
clips.modifications: Trimmed; decoded from MP3 and converted to mono 44.1 kHz 16-bit WAV. No filtering or gain change.
clips.notes: Classified as gobble by measurement: a single ~0.95 s burst of rapid broadband pulses, energy peak about 1.4-3 kHz, far louder than anything else (40-60 dB above the noise floor); xeno-canto type 'song', sex 'male', remarks say 'gobbling'. Male seen <10 m away (recordist remarks). Clean, close bird. Followed 1.4 s later by the 'click' the recordist mentions; the click is outside the trim. Peak sample 0.56 of full scale (not clipped).

clips.author: Richard E. Webster
clips.modifications: Trimmed; decoded from MP3 (48 kHz stereo) and converted to mono 44.1 kHz 16-bit WAV (stereo channels averaged). No filtering or gain change.
clips.notes: Classified as yelp by measurement, not confirmed by an expert or by the recordist (xeno-canto type: 'call'). Measured: a regular series of about 11 notes, one every ~0.29 s. Each note starts high (~2.2 kHz, partial at ~3.2 kHz) and breaks down to a lower part at ~1.2-1.3 kHz: a two-part note repeated as a series, matching the yelp description. First note ~0.4 s into the clip (lead-in for the noise floor). Peak sample 0.26 of full scale (not clipped). Same session as yelp-2/3, so the three yelps may be one or two birds. Recordist remarks: four birds, seemingly two young males doing most of the calling, and two females; animal seen, no playback; 2022-12-26, San Bernardino National Wildlife Refuge, Cochise County, Arizona. Call definition used: the yelp is a series of single notes, often heard as a two-part 'kee-yuk' (NWTF 'The Sounds of the Wild Turkey'; Outdoor Life turkey sounds guide; read via web-search excerpts, pages not opened from the build environment).

clips.author: Richard E. Webster
clips.modifications: Trimmed; decoded from MP3 (48 kHz mono) and converted to mono 44.1 kHz 16-bit WAV. No filtering or gain change.
clips.notes: Classified as kee-kee-run by measurement, not confirmed by an expert or by the recordist (xeno-canto type: 'call'). Measured: first ~0.4 s quiet, then about 6 steady tonal whistles (~1.55-1.75 kHz, with a second band near 1.95 kHz) over ~2.3 s, then from ~2.85 s a series of about 8 yelp-like notes (~2.2 kHz breaking to ~1.3 kHz, ~0.3 s apart). Whistles followed by yelps, matching the kee kee run description; recordist context (birds separated from the flock) fits. Creek noise throughout. Peak sample 0.12 (not clipped). Recordist remarks: at least two birds trying to re-unite with each other and the rest of the flock (about 12 more birds) from which they had become separated; noisy creek; interval shortened at 1:01, 3:19 and 4:08 (outside this clip); animal seen, no playback; 2020-04-16, Portal, Arizona. Call definition used: the kee kee is a high, whistle-like call of young birds separated from the flock; the kee kee run is a kee kee followed by yelps (South Carolina DNR turkey sounds page, NWTF; read via web-search excerpts, pages not opened from the build environment).
